drometrizole-trisiloxane.summary: Photostable UVA/UVB sunscreen filter (Mexoryl XL) that helps daily sunscreen keep protecting skin from sun-driven aging and uneven tone.

quick.overview:
Drometrizole trisiloxane, sold as Mexoryl XL, is an organic UV filter that absorbs both UVB and UVA light. People look for it in daily sunscreens because steady UV protection keeps skin tone more even and slows sun-driven aging.

It absorbs UV (peaks near 303 nm and 344 nm) and converts it to less harmful energy within the sunscreen film. It is usually formulated with ecamsule (Mexoryl SX). Published work is mostly formulation, photoprotection and contact-allergy research on finished products rather than trials of cosmetic outcomes.
quick.how: It is an ingredient in L'Oreal-group sunscreens and daily-wear skincare, applied as part of a morning facial sunscreen or SPF moisturiser. It is approved in the EU, Canada, Australia and Japan but not in the United States, so people in the US who want it usually buy imported products.
quick.risks: Case reports describe allergic contact dermatitis to it. It is not an approved US sunscreen active, so US availability depends on imports or products using other filters.

angle.text: Drometrizole trisiloxane (Mexoryl XL) is a photostable UVA and UVB filter in L'Oreal-brand sunscreens, often paired with ecamsule. Because it keeps absorbing light through the day, daily use helps limit the photoaging and uneven tone that sun exposure builds up. Published work covers formulation and regulatory data rather than appearance trials.

enzacamene.summary: Camphor-derived UVB sunscreen filter (4-MBC) once used to protect skin from sun aging, now banned in EU cosmetics over endocrine-activity findings.

quick.overview:
Enzacamene (4-MBC) is an organic UVB filter that was used in sunscreens, especially in Europe, to reduce sunburn and the photodamage behind sunspots and wrinkles.

It absorbs UVB and dissipates the energy partly through cis-trans isomerisation, though its photostability is described as limited. Regulators moved against it after lab and animal studies reported estrogenic and thyroid effects, and the EU SCCS found sufficient evidence of endocrine disruption in 2022. Appearance outcomes were not studied for it specifically.
quick.how: It appeared as one ingredient among several filters in SPF products. Today it mostly comes up when people check ingredient lists and regional availability; it remains permitted in some countries, such as Canada, while the EU banned it in cosmetics in 2024 and the US never approved it.
quick.risks: Lab and animal studies reported estrogenic and thyroid effects, and human studies detected it in plasma, urine and milk. It is banned in EU cosmetics and reportedly in the UK and China, and is not FDA-approved.

angle.text: Enzacamene (4-MBC) is an older camphor-derived UVB filter that was used in sunscreens to cut sunburn and the photodamage that leads to sunspots and wrinkles. It is now banned in EU cosmetics, so it mainly comes up when people check ingredient lists. Appearance outcomes were not studied for it specifically.

amiloxate.summary: Cinnamate UVB sunscreen filter, EU-approved since 1997, that helps protect skin from sunburn and gradual photoaging.

quick.overview:
Amiloxate is a cinnamate-type UVB filter found in some sunscreens. People use sunscreens with filters like it to prevent sunburn and the cumulative photoaging that shows up as uneven tone and wrinkles.

It absorbs UVB radiation within the sunscreen film. Published work on it is mostly analytical and environmental, plus case reports of photoallergic contact dermatitis; its appearance benefit follows from the general effect of sunscreens.
quick.how: It is an ingredient in EU sunscreens, usually combined with other filters in a daily or holiday SPF. Benefits come from regular application over months and years rather than from a visible change after one use.
quick.risks: Photoallergic contact dermatitis has been reported. It is not an approved US OTC sunscreen active.

angle.text: Amiloxate is a cinnamate UVB filter found in EU sunscreens. By absorbing UVB it lowers sunburn, and over time less sun damage means skin stays more even and youthful. Published work on it consists mainly of analytical studies and photoallergy case reports.

bisdisulizole-disodium.summary: Water-soluble UVA sunscreen filter (Neo Heliopan AP), EU-approved since 2000, used for light textures that protect against UVA-linked wrinkles and dark spots.

quick.overview:
Bisdisulizole disodium is a water-soluble UVA filter sold by Symrise as Neo Heliopan AP. It lets formulators make light, easy-to-wear sun protection against the UVA rays tied to wrinkles and dark spots.

It absorbs UVA radiation in the sunscreen formulation. It has been approved in the EU at up to 10% since 2000; few sources document it in detail, and the evidence is regulatory and formulation-based rather than appearance trials.
quick.how: It appears in EU sunscreens and facial SPF products with light textures suited to daily wear, typically alongside other filters that cover UVB. It is not approved in the US.
quick.risks: No dedicated safety information was found in the sources reviewed, and it is not approved in the United States.

angle.text: Bisdisulizole disodium (Neo Heliopan AP) is a water-soluble UVA filter in EU sunscreens. It allows light textures that suit daily facial wear and protect against UVA-linked wrinkles and dark spots. Evidence is regulatory and formulation-based rather than appearance trials.

meradimate.summary: Older anthranilate UVA sunscreen filter listed in US sunscreen rules that adds UVA coverage against sun aging.

quick.overview:
Meradimate (menthyl anthranilate) is a UVA filter used to add UVA coverage in sunscreens, helping protect skin from the sun damage that drives photoaging.

It absorbs UVA light and has been characterised as fluorescent, with studies mapping its excited-state behaviour. It is one of the 17 ingredients the FDA lists for OTC sunscreens. Research on it is mainly photophysical and in vitro; no clinical outcome trials were found.
quick.how: It is used in some products alongside other filters, for example a US sports sunscreen listing it with octinoxate, octisalate and oxybenzone. It works as part of a combined filter system in daily or outdoor SPF.
quick.risks: Labels advise stopping use if rash occurs. Lab studies have examined cell effects and sperm-signalling interactions of UV filters; no clinical outcome data were found.

angle.text: Meradimate is an older anthranilate UVA filter listed in US sunscreen rules, used to add UVA coverage that helps protect skin from sun aging. It has been studied mostly for its photophysics rather than for appearance outcomes.

padimate-o.summary: Older PABA-derived UVB filter once common in sunscreens and lip products to protect against sun damage, now rarely used.

quick.overview:
Padimate O is an oily PABA-derived UVB filter that was common in sunscreens and lip products to prevent sunburn and sun-driven skin aging.

It absorbs UVB light. Researchers have debated its photochemistry: in vitro work suggested indirect DNA damage on irradiation, while hairless-mouse studies reported no carcinogenic effect. It is approved by the US FDA among other agencies, and appearance outcomes were not studied for it specifically.
quick.how: It was used as one filter in SPF creams and lip balms. It is less common now and mostly appears in ingredient-history discussions.
quick.risks: Yeast and cell studies raised photomutagenicity and hormone-receptor questions, while hairless-mouse studies found no carcinogenicity. Labels advise stopping use if rash occurs.

angle.text: Padimate O is an older PABA-derived UVB filter once common in sunscreens and lip products. By absorbing UVB it cuts sunburn and the sun damage behind premature skin aging. It is rarely used now, and appearance outcomes were not studied for it specifically.

paba.summary: The original UVB sunscreen filter, patented in 1943, which helped prevent burning and sun-aged skin before modern formulas replaced it.

quick.overview:
PABA was one of the first chemical sunscreen ingredients, patented in 1943, and was widely used in mid-century suncare to prevent burning and sun-aged skin.

It absorbs UVB (about 290 to 320 nm) and passes most UVA. Its use fell after reports of allergic contact dermatitis, photocontact dermatitis and clothing stains, and early-1980s lab work suggested it could sensitise cells to UV damage. Long-term appearance trials of PABA are not available.
quick.how: Today it is mostly encountered as history, as the ingredient modern sunscreens moved away from. Water-insoluble derivatives such as padimate O have continued in some cosmetics, and PABA itself also occurs naturally in foods like liver, yeast and whole grains.
quick.risks: Documented risks include allergic contact dermatitis, photocontact dermatitis and eye irritation. The EU banned it as a sunscreen ingredient in 2008, and the US FDA proposed limited allowance in 2019.

angle.text: PABA was one of the first sunscreen actives, used for decades to prevent burning and sun-aged skin. It absorbs UVB light, and less UV damage means less photoaging over time. It is now known mainly as the ingredient modern formulas moved away from.

cinoxate.summary: Older cinnamate UVB sunscreen filter, US-approved in 1961, used to protect skin from sun damage and now rarely used.

quick.overview:
Cinoxate is a cinnamate-based UVB filter that the US FDA approved in 1961. It appeared in some older sunscreens to reduce sunburn and photodamage.

As a methoxycinnamic acid ester it absorbs UVB in the skin's surface layers. A 2023 review cited by Wikipedia describes it as no longer commonly used in cosmetics, and its appearance effect was not studied separately.
quick.how: It was used as one filter among others in SPF products. It now mainly shows up in ingredient lists and history.
quick.risks: No human safety trials are documented in the sources. A 1989 cell study reported increased chromosome changes when combined with other agents, and a 2024 computational study predicted PPAR-gamma activity.

angle.text: Cinoxate is an older cinnamate UVB filter, US-approved in 1961, that appeared in some sunscreens. Absorbing UVB reduces sunburn and photodamage, which supports skin that ages more slowly. It is rarely used now.

dioxybenzone.summary: Benzophenone sunscreen filter (benzophenone-8) listed in the US monograph that adds UVB and short-UVA coverage against sun aging.

quick.overview:
Dioxybenzone (benzophenone-8) is a UV filter that absorbs UVB and short-wave UVA, adding coverage that helps protect skin from sun aging. It appears in the US sunscreen monograph.

Its benzophenone core absorbs ultraviolet light and dissipates the energy, the same general mechanism as other benzophenone filters. Very little published research addresses it specifically, so its appearance benefit follows from sunscreens in general.
quick.how: It is used as one component in a combined filter system in sunscreens. Dedicated information on routines or results for dioxybenzone itself is sparse.
quick.risks: No dioxybenzone-specific human safety data appear in the sources. Studies of benzophenones as a class, mainly oxybenzone, have looked at environmental presence, coral toxicity and cell-level hormone activity.

angle.text: Dioxybenzone (benzophenone-8) is a sunscreen filter in the US monograph that adds UVB and short-UVA coverage, protecting skin from sun-driven aging. It has almost no dedicated research, so its benefit is inferred from sunscreens as a class.

sulisobenzone.summary: Water-soluble benzophenone UV filter (BP-4) in sunscreens and hair products that protects skin and dyed hair from UV damage.

quick.overview:
Sulisobenzone (benzophenone-4) absorbs UVB and short UVA and, unlike other benzophenones, dissolves in water. People encounter it in sunscreens for skin protection and in hair products meant to protect colour and structure.

Its benzophenone structure absorbs UV, and the sulfonic acid group makes it water-soluble. Most published work concerns its presence in rivers and wastewater rather than human appearance trials.
quick.how: It is an ingredient in some sunscreens and in some hair products such as colour-protecting sprays, used as part of a daily routine alongside other filters.
quick.risks: No dedicated human safety trials appear in the sources reviewed. Environmental studies report it in surface water, and UV filters as a class have been tested for hormone-like activity in cells and fish.

angle.text: Sulisobenzone (benzophenone-4) is a water-soluble UV filter in some sunscreens and in hair products meant to protect colour and structure. Less UV damage means less photoaging of skin and less fading of dyed hair. Research on it is mostly environmental.

trolamine-salicylate.summary: Salicylate best known as the active in odourless muscle-pain creams, historically also a weak UVB absorber in sunscreens.

quick.overview:
Trolamine salicylate is a salicylate salt best known as the active ingredient in over-the-counter topical pain creams. It has also been used as a weak UVB filter in sunscreens and cosmetics, which is its minor link to skin protection.

The salicylate part absorbs UVB, and triethanolamine neutralises the acid. In 2019 the US FDA proposed that its sunscreen use is not generally recognised as safe and effective. Small trials from the 1980s and 1990s studied it for knee osteoarthritis and exercise-induced soreness, with mixed results.
quick.how: People mostly use it as an odourless rub for aches in muscles and joints. As a sunscreen ingredient it appeared in older formulas as a supporting filter.
quick.risks: Labels say external use only. Listed hazards include eye damage and skin or eye irritation. Absorbed salicylate has been measured in blood after topical use in a small human study.

angle.text: Trolamine salicylate is best known as the active in odourless muscle-pain creams, and was historically used as a weak UVB absorber in sunscreens and cosmetics. Its link to appearance is minor: the salicylate absorbs some UVB, which gave it an occasional supporting role in older sun products.

polysilicone-15.summary: Silicone-polymer UVB filter (Parsol SLX) in sunscreens, lip balms and hair products that protects skin, lips and treated hair from sun.

quick.overview:
Polysilicone-15 is a large silicone-based UVB filter sold as Parsol SLX. It is used in sunscreens, lip balms and some hair products, so people can protect skin, lips and colour-treated hair from sun damage.

It absorbs UVB light with a maximum near 310 nm, and its polymer-like size is intended to keep it on the skin's surface. An in vitro study covered it among 18 EU filters, and published safety data are limited to a few case reports.
quick.how: It is applied as part of a sunscreen, lip balm with SPF, or hair product, usually combined with other filters. It is approved in the EU.
quick.risks: Case reports describe allergic contact dermatitis and cheilitis. No controlled clinical trials are documented.

angle.text: Polysilicone-15 (Parsol SLX) is a UVB filter used in EU sunscreens, lip balms and hair products, so users can protect skin, lips and colour-treated hair from sun. Less UV damage supports skin that ages more slowly. Published work is formulation data and case reports rather than appearance trials.

tris-biphenyl-triazine.summary: Newer particulate UV filter (Tinosorb A2B) that gives daily sunscreens broad UVB and UVA coverage against photoaging and pigmentation.

quick.overview:
Tris-biphenyl triazine is a synthetic UV filter sold as Tinosorb A2B. Skincare enthusiasts look for it in daily-wear sunscreens for broad coverage against the photoaging and pigmentation that sun exposure causes.

It is a particulate triazine-class filter that absorbs UVB and UVA and also scatters some light, described as a recent addition to the filters authorised in Europe. It has also been tested as a photostabilizer for avobenzone. Published work is laboratory and formulation research; no human trials of its effect on skin appearance were found.
quick.how: It is an ingredient in sunscreen formulations, typically combined with other filters in a daily facial SPF. Approval and permitted concentrations differ by country.
quick.risks: No compound-specific human safety trials were found. Approval and maximum concentrations vary by country, and UV filters as a class are the subject of ongoing safety and environmental assessment.

angle.text: Tris-biphenyl triazine (Tinosorb A2B) is a newer particulate filter that skincare enthusiasts look for in daily-wear sunscreens. It absorbs UVB and UVA and scatters some light, so protection against photoaging and pigmentation stays broad. Research so far is laboratory and formulation work.

methoxypropylamino-cyclohexenylidene-eth.summary: L'Oreal's long-wave UVA1 filter (Mexoryl 400 / UVMune), EU-approved in 2019, aimed at the UVA tied to wrinkles and dark spots.

quick.overview:
This filter, abbreviated MCE, absorbs long-wave UVA1 (360 to 400 nm, peak 385 nm), the range tied to wrinkling and pigmentation. L'Oreal markets it as Mexoryl 400, and La Roche-Posay sells it as UVMune.

It was developed by L'Oreal and BASF. The EU approved it in 2019 at up to 3%, and Australia followed in 2025. No peer-reviewed clinical studies of the filter were found.
quick.how: It is used in La Roche-Posay and other L'Oreal-group sunscreens, as part of a daily facial SPF with other filters. Per Wikipedia it is used only in L'Oreal-group products.
quick.risks: Public toxicology information is limited to regulatory opinions and concentration limits. The US FDA does not currently recognise it for sunscreens.

angle.text: This L'Oreal filter (Mexoryl 400, UVMune) targets long-wave UVA1, the range tied to wrinkling and pigmentation, and is promoted in La Roche-Posay sunscreens. It gained EU approval in 2019; no published human trials show appearance outcomes.

phenylene-bis-diphenyltriazine.summary: Newer triazine filter (TriAsorB) its developers say covers UVB, UVA and blue light to limit sun-driven pigmentation and aging.

quick.overview:
Phenylene bis-diphenyltriazine, sold as TriAsorB, is a newer triazine-class filter that its developers say covers UVB, UVA and high-energy blue light. It appeals to people worried about pigmentation and aging from sun and visible light.

Developer-authored papers describe it as a new-generation filter and report SPF50+ formulations containing it. Human studies are few and come largely from groups associated with its development; they examine blue-light-induced pigmentation and testing methods. The EU SCCS published a safety opinion in 2018.
quick.how: It is used as an ingredient in sunscreen formulations, often listed alongside bemotrizinol and tris-biphenyl triazine, as part of a daily SPF. Approval varies by jurisdiction.
quick.risks: No independent long-term human safety trials were found, and approval varies by jurisdiction.

angle.text: Phenylene bis-diphenyltriazine (TriAsorB) is a newer filter its developers say covers UVB, UVA and high-energy blue light, which appeals to users worried about sun-driven pigmentation and aging. Studies so far come mostly from groups linked to its development.

titanium-dioxide.summary: Classic mineral UV filter and white pigment in physical sunscreens and tinted SPF that protects skin from sun aging and evens tone.

quick.overview:
Titanium dioxide is a white mineral used as a physical sunscreen filter and as a pigment in tinted SPF. It protects against the sun damage behind photoaging and gives tinted products a more even look for the day.

It scatters and reflects light and absorbs UV, giving good UVB and UVA II coverage but weaker UVA I coverage. With zinc oxide it was the only filter the FDA recognised as GRASE as of 2021. Larger particles can leave a white cast, while nano-sized particles give a sheerer finish.
quick.how: It is used in mineral sunscreens and tinted SPF, usually paired with zinc oxide, as a daily facial or body sunscreen. People who prefer mineral over organic filters often choose it.
quick.risks: IARC classes inhaled dust as Group 2B and advises against sprayable sunscreens. The EU removed it as a food additive in 2022, which does not concern sunscreen use. Non-nano particles mostly stay in the outer skin layer, though nanoparticle effects on aquatic life are studied.

angle.text: Titanium dioxide is the classic mineral sunscreen filter and white pigment, used in physical sunscreens and tinted SPF to protect skin from sun aging and even out tone for the day. It gives good UVB and UVA II protection and is weaker on long UVA.

zinc-oxide.summary: Mineral UV filter and skin protectant with broad UVA/UVB coverage, used for gentle sun protection and in barrier creams.

quick.overview:
Zinc oxide is a mineral powder used as a sunscreen filter and as a skin protectant in diaper-rash and barrier creams. People choose it for gentle, photostable protection that helps keep skin even and youthful.

It absorbs UV light because of its wide band gap and also scatters some. Wikipedia calls it the broadest-spectrum UVA and UVB absorber among sunscreen filters and describes it as completely photostable. As of 2021 it and titanium dioxide were the only FDA-recognised GRASE filters; the EU approved it as a UV filter in 2016.
quick.how: It is used in mineral sunscreens, often with titanium dioxide, and in barrier ointments and calamine lotion. Larger particles leave a white cast, so many modern sunscreens use nanoparticle forms, covered in a separate entry.
quick.risks: It is generally described as non-irritating and non-comedogenic. Inhaled fumes can cause metal fume fever, and nano forms are studied for effects on aquatic life.

angle.text: Zinc oxide is a broad-spectrum mineral sunscreen filter used by people seeking gentle, photostable protection that preserves youthful, even skin. It also forms the base of barrier creams. Less UV damage over time is how it supports appearance.

nano-zinc-oxide.summary: Nanoparticle zinc oxide: the transparent version of the mineral filter that protects against UV without a white cast.

quick.overview:
Nano zinc oxide is zinc oxide in nanometre-sized particles, used so mineral sunscreens go on transparent instead of white while still protecting skin from sun aging.

The small size permits higher loadings without a white cast, and particles are often coated, for example with silica, to limit reactivity. It reflects, scatters and absorbs UVA and UVB. Human studies summarised in reference works report particles staying in the outer skin layer. No studies of appearance outcomes were found.
quick.how: It is used in sheer mineral sunscreens and tinted or daily-wear SPF, where a clear finish makes regular application easier. In the EU such products carry a nano label; the US does not require one.
quick.risks: Laboratory studies report cytotoxicity and aquatic toxicity linked to dissolved zinc and reactive oxygen species. The debate centres on skin penetration and environmental effects.

angle.text: Nano zinc oxide is the transparent version of the mineral filter, used so mineral sunscreens go on without a white cast while still protecting skin from sun aging. The sheer finish is visible straight away; the debate is about penetration and aquatic toxicity.

nano-titanium-dioxide.summary: Sheer nanoscale mineral UV filter that lets sunscreens go on without a chalky cast and supports protection against sun aging.

quick.overview:
Nano titanium dioxide is a very fine mineral powder used in sunscreens to absorb and scatter UV light. Its small particles make mineral sunscreens look sheerer than older chalky formulas, which makes daily wear easier and supports protection against sunburn and photoaging.

As a wide-bandgap semiconductor it absorbs UV below about 400 nm and scatters little visible light at nanoscale sizes. Under UV it can also generate reactive oxygen species, the basis of its photocatalytic uses. A 2010 review addressed nano titanium dioxide and zinc oxide in sunscreens specifically; no sunscreen-specific clinical trials were found.
quick.how: It is used in mineral sunscreens, often alongside ultrafine zinc oxide, by people who prefer mineral over organic filters. It is applied as a daily facial or body sunscreen.
quick.risks: IARC classifies inhaled TiO2 dust as Group 2B and advises against sprayable sunscreens. Laboratory studies report gut-barrier and ecological effects at tested exposures. The EU banned it as a food additive in 2022; sunscreen use is regulated separately.

angle.text: Nano titanium dioxide is used in modern mineral sunscreens so they look sheer rather than chalky, which makes daily wear easier and supports protection against sun aging. The nano-specific safety debate continues.

cerium-oxide.summary: Industrial ceramic oxide discussed as a low-photoreactivity mineral UV absorber for sunscreens, with antioxidant nanoceria research.

quick.overview:
Cerium oxide is a pale powder mostly used to polish glass and in catalysts. It has been suggested as a sunscreen ingredient because it absorbs UV with less photoreactivity than zinc or titanium oxide, which would suit products aimed at preventing sun-driven skin aging.

UV absorption comes from its semiconductor-like oxide lattice. Most research is on nanoparticle versions (nanoceria), which flip between Ce3+ and Ce4+ states and mimic antioxidant enzymes in the lab. No human trials of cerium oxide as a sunscreen or appearance product were found.
quick.how: It is a candidate ingredient in cosmetics discussions rather than a staple of mainstream sunscreens. Wikipedia describes nanoceria as a prospective replacement for zinc oxide and titanium dioxide in sunscreens.
quick.risks: No human sunscreen trials were found. Laboratory work shows low cell toxicity in some models, but nanoparticle safety on skin has not been clinically established.

angle.text: Cerium oxide is discussed as a mineral UV absorber with lower photocatalytic activity than zinc oxide or titanium dioxide, which would suit sunscreens aimed at preventing skin aging. Antioxidant nanoceria research exists; human sunscreen studies do not.
